modulePurpose: Optional organizational-level defensive governance, incident prioritization and risk assessment scenarios.
prerequisite: Complete at least 10 Advanced first attempts with at least 75% first-attempt accuracy. This is a practice heuristic, not a competency certification.

questions.title: Containment Under Uncertainty
questions.learningObjective: Prioritize coordinated containment, evidence preservation and decision ownership during an active multi-system incident.
questions.scenario: At 09:10, the security operations centre receives three correlated alerts: an endpoint has begun encrypting files, a service account has authenticated from an unusual location, and outbound traffic from a file server has increased sharply. The incident commander has not yet confirmed the initial access path. A business unit asks to power off every server immediately.
questions.question: What is the strongest first coordinated decision for the incident commander?

options.text: Declare a major incident, activate the response plan, isolate confirmed affected systems using approved procedures, preserve relevant telemetry, and scope related accounts and hosts before broader disruptive action.
Power off every server and workstation immediately, then begin evidence collection after systems restart.
Wait until the initial access path is proven before changing any network or account state.
Ask the affected business unit to negotiate directly with the suspected attacker while IT investigates.

questions.correctAnswer: Declare a major incident, activate the response plan, isolate confirmed affected systems using approved procedures, preserve relevant telemetry, and scope related accounts and hosts before broader disruptive action.

A.explanation: Correct. Coordinated activation, proportionate containment, evidence preservation and scoping support an informed response while limiting unnecessary operational disruption.

B.explanation: A blanket shutdown can destroy volatile evidence and disrupt unaffected services. Review the evidence, use approved organizational controls and avoid treating an alert or familiar message as proof.

C.explanation: Waiting for attribution can allow active damage to continue. Review the evidence, use approved organizational controls and avoid treating an alert or familiar message as proof.

D.explanation: Direct uncoordinated contact bypasses the authorized response structure. Review the evidence, use approved organizational controls and avoid treating an alert or familiar message as proof.

questions.explanation: Correct. Coordinated activation, proportionate containment, evidence preservation and scoping support an informed response while limiting unnecessary operational disruption.
questions.keyTakeaway: Act on credible indicators through the incident plan; do not wait for perfect attribution or take uncontrolled disruptive action.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Activate the approved incident-response process, appoint a decision owner, preserve logs and volatile evidence where feasible, isolate confirmed affected assets, scope identity and network activity, and record decisions and uncertainties.
questions.difficultyRationale: Expert: requires sequencing containment, evidence preservation, uncertainty management and business coordination.

questions.title: The Critical Supplier Component
questions.learningObjective: Prioritize a supplier vulnerability using exposure, exploitability, criticality, provenance and compensating controls.
questions.scenario: A supplier notifies the organization that a widely used authentication component has a critical vulnerability. The component appears in the software bill of materials for six services. Two services are internet-facing; one supports payroll. There is no confirmed exploitation in your environment, and the vendor has published a mitigation plus a target patch date.
questions.question: Which response best balances urgency, evidence and business continuity?

options.text: Immediately disable all six services, regardless of exposure or business impact, and defer risk review.
Record the notification as informational until the vendor confirms exploitation against your organization.

Use the SBOM and asset inventory to identify deployed versions and reachable exposure, prioritize critical services, apply the vendor mitigation or approved compensating controls, test and deploy the patch through change control, and track residual risk.
Ask each service owner to independently decide whether the component matters, without central coordination or an owner for remediation.

questions.correctAnswer: Use the SBOM and asset inventory to identify deployed versions and reachable exposure, prioritize critical services, apply the vendor mitigation or approved compensating controls, test and deploy the patch through change control, and track residual risk.

A.explanation: Disabling every service without triage can cause avoidable business harm. Review the evidence, use approved organizational controls and avoid treating an alert or familiar message as proof.

B.explanation: Waiting for confirmed compromise delays preventive risk treatment. Review the evidence, use approved organizational controls and avoid treating an alert or familiar message as proof.

C.explanation: Correct. Component inventory, exposure and criticality support defensible prioritization; mitigation, controlled patching and residual-risk tracking maintain accountability.

D.explanation: Uncoordinated service-owner decisions can create remediation gaps. Review the evidence, use approved organizational controls and avoid treating an alert or familiar message as proof.

questions.explanation: Correct. Component inventory, exposure and criticality support defensible prioritization; mitigation, controlled patching and residual-risk tracking maintain accountability.
questions.keyTakeaway: A component inventory becomes actionable when it is connected to deployed assets, exposure, criticality and accountable remediation.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Correlate SBOM entries with asset and service inventories; validate affected versions; rank by exposure and business criticality; apply vendor guidance; test patches; coordinate change windows; document residual risk and supplier follow-up.
questions.difficultyRationale: Expert: integrates software supply-chain visibility, asset criticality, remediation planning and risk ownership.

questions.title: An Insider-Risk Signal
questions.learningObjective: Respond to potential insider-risk indicators using objective evidence, privacy safeguards, least privilege and authorized processes.
questions.scenario: A manager reports that an employee has downloaded an unusually large number of project files shortly before transferring teams. The employee’s role includes legitimate access to many of those files. A second alert shows that a removable device was connected, but the device contents are not yet known.
questions.question: What is the most defensible organizational response?

options.text: Publicly accuse the employee and ask colleagues to search their personal accounts for evidence.
Treat the alerts as a confirmed malicious insider incident and terminate access permanently without review.
Ignore the alerts because the employee’s role permits access to the files.

Preserve relevant audit records, validate the activity against role and business context, involve the authorized security, HR, privacy and legal stakeholders under policy, and apply proportionate, approved access controls while the facts are assessed.

questions.correctAnswer: Preserve relevant audit records, validate the activity against role and business context, involve the authorized security, HR, privacy and legal stakeholders under policy, and apply proportionate, approved access controls while the facts are assessed.

A.explanation: Public accusation and informal searches can violate privacy and compromise evidence. Review the evidence, use approved organizational controls and avoid treating an alert or familiar message as proof.

B.explanation: Alerts alone do not establish malicious intent. Review the evidence, use approved organizational controls and avoid treating an alert or familiar message as proof.

C.explanation: Authorized access does not make anomalous activity automatically benign. Review the evidence, use approved organizational controls and avoid treating an alert or familiar message as proof.

D.explanation: Correct. Objective validation, evidence preservation, multidisciplinary oversight and proportionate controls protect both the organization and individual rights.

questions.explanation: Correct. Objective validation, evidence preservation, multidisciplinary oversight and proportionate controls protect both the organization and individual rights.
questions.keyTakeaway: Insider-risk indicators require evidence-led assessment, not assumptions about intent or identity.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Preserve relevant logs, validate activity against job duties and approved work, restrict access only when authorized and proportionate, and coordinate with designated security, HR, privacy and legal functions.
questions.difficultyRationale: Expert: balances threat detection, due process, privacy, evidence and least-privilege access.

questions.category: Business email compromise and financial controls
questions.title: The Executive Payment Change
questions.learningObjective: Interrupt payment diversion using independent verification, separation of duties and timely financial institution notification.
questions.scenario: Finance receives an email in an existing supplier thread requesting that a large invoice be paid to a new bank account. The message appears to come from the supplier’s known address. The CFO separately messages the finance lead asking for the payment to be expedited and says the supplier is waiting.
questions.question: What is the correct control response before any payment is released?

options.text: Reply to the email thread asking the sender to confirm the new account number.

Pause the payment and verify the change through a previously established, independently sourced supplier contact; require the organization’s documented dual-approval process and report the suspicious request through security and finance channels.
Release a small test payment to the new account, then wait for the supplier to confirm receipt.
Accept the change because the email is part of a legitimate historical supplier thread and the CFO requested urgency.

questions.correctAnswer: Pause the payment and verify the change through a previously established, independently sourced supplier contact; require the organization’s documented dual-approval process and report the suspicious request through security and finance channels.

A.explanation: A compromised mailbox can control replies in the same email thread. Review the evidence, use approved organizational controls and avoid treating an alert or familiar message as proof.

B.explanation: Correct. A trusted out-of-band verification path and separation of duties reduce the risk of payment diversion and create an auditable approval trail.

C.explanation: A test transfer can still be lost without authenticating the new account. Review the evidence, use approved organizational controls and avoid treating an alert or familiar message as proof.

D.explanation: A familiar thread and executive urgency do not authenticate changed bank details. Review the evidence, use approved organizational controls and avoid treating an alert or familiar message as proof.

questions.explanation: Correct. A trusted out-of-band verification path and separation of duties reduce the risk of payment diversion and create an auditable approval trail.
questions.keyTakeaway: A payment-detail change is a high-risk request even when it arrives inside a familiar email conversation.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Place the payment on hold, call a previously verified supplier contact using a trusted directory or existing contract record, follow dual authorization, retain evidence and notify the organization’s security/finance process. If money has already moved, contact the bank immediately and report through the appropriate channels.
questions.difficultyRationale: Expert: combines identity verification, payment controls, executive pressure and incident escalation.

questions.title: The Board Risk Briefing
questions.learningObjective: Communicate incident facts, uncertainty, business impact and decisions to leadership without overstating attribution or assurance.
questions.scenario: A board meeting is scheduled two hours after a suspected compromise of a customer-facing platform. The response team has isolated two hosts, but the scope of data access is still under investigation. The board chair asks for a definitive statement that no customer data was accessed and wants an exact recovery time.
questions.question: What should the incident lead present?

options.text: State that no data was accessed because no exfiltration has been confirmed, and promise the service will be restored within two hours.
Avoid briefing the board until forensic analysis has established the attacker’s identity and complete timeline.

Provide verified facts, known business impacts, containment already taken, current unknowns and confidence levels; explain next decision points, accountable owners, communication/legal review paths and a time for the next update rather than making unsupported assurances.
Share raw security logs and speculate about the likely attacker to demonstrate technical transparency.

questions.correctAnswer: Provide verified facts, known business impacts, containment already taken, current unknowns and confidence levels; explain next decision points, accountable owners, communication/legal review paths and a time for the next update rather than making unsupported assurances.

A.explanation: No confirmed exfiltration does not prove that data was not accessed. Review the evidence, use approved organizational controls and avoid treating an alert or familiar message as proof.

B.explanation: Leadership needs timely decision-ready information before attribution is complete. Review the evidence, use approved organizational controls and avoid treating an alert or familiar message as proof.

C.explanation: Correct. Clear separation of verified facts, assumptions and unknowns supports governance decisions without overstating certainty.

D.explanation: Raw logs and attacker speculation can expose sensitive information and mislead leaders. Review the evidence, use approved organizational controls and avoid treating an alert or familiar message as proof.

questions.explanation: Correct. Clear separation of verified facts, assumptions and unknowns supports governance decisions without overstating certainty.
questions.keyTakeaway: Good incident governance makes uncertainty visible and assigns decisions; it does not conceal uncertainty or turn it into assurance.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Use a structured incident briefing: what happened, what is confirmed, what remains unknown, business impact, actions taken, decisions needed, owner and next update time. Coordinate external and regulatory communications with authorized stakeholders.
questions.difficultyRationale: Expert: tests executive communication, risk governance, uncertainty and decision accountability.

questions.title: Recovering After Ransomware
questions.learningObjective: Sequence recovery using containment, clean restoration sources, identity assurance, validation and monitored return to service.
questions.scenario: A ransomware incident has been contained. Several production servers are encrypted, the backup platform was reachable from part of the affected environment, and an offline backup set is available. Executives want the customer portal restored first. The incident team has not yet validated the backup set or rotated potentially exposed credentials.
questions.question: Which recovery sequence is most defensible?

options.text: Validate and protect clean backup sources, establish a trusted recovery environment, address compromised identities and access paths, restore prioritized services in a controlled order, test integrity and security, then monitor closely before declaring recovery.
Restore the customer portal immediately from the most recent backup, then investigate whether the backup was affected.
Pay the ransom first so the attacker can provide a decryption key, then use it as the primary recovery plan.
Reconnect all affected servers at once after encryption stops, because the incident is already contained.

questions.correctAnswer: Validate and protect clean backup sources, establish a trusted recovery environment, address compromised identities and access paths, restore prioritized services in a controlled order, test integrity and security, then monitor closely before declaring recovery.

A.explanation: Correct. Recovery depends on trustworthy restoration sources, a clean environment, identity/access remediation, prioritized validation and monitoring.

B.explanation: The newest backup may also be encrypted, compromised or contaminated. Review the evidence, use approved organizational controls and avoid treating an alert or familiar message as proof.

C.explanation: Payment does not guarantee decryption, recovery or prevention of data disclosure. Review the evidence, use approved organizational controls and avoid treating an alert or familiar message as proof.

D.explanation: Stopped encryption does not prove attacker access or persistence is gone. Review the evidence, use approved organizational controls and avoid treating an alert or familiar message as proof.

questions.explanation: Correct. Recovery depends on trustworthy restoration sources, a clean environment, identity/access remediation, prioritized validation and monitoring.
questions.keyTakeaway: Recovery is not simply restoring files; it is returning services to a known-good, validated and monitored state.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Follow the organization’s recovery plan, validate offline or otherwise trusted backups, rebuild or restore in a clean environment, reset affected credentials and tokens as appropriate, prioritize services by business impact, test security and integrity, and monitor after restoration.
questions.difficultyRationale: Expert: integrates recovery sequencing, backup assurance, identity remediation, business continuity and validation.
